newsitem.title: UK: UK Jan inflation not enough to trigger rate rise.
newsitem.headline: UK Jan inflation not enough to trigger rate rise.

text.p: Stubbornly high British inflation is a growing worry for financial markets, but with political factors apparently outweighing all else, the latest data are unlikely to spark a swift rise in interest rates, analysts said.
Headline inflation rose to 2.8 percent in January from 2.5 percent in December and underlying inflation stuck at 3.1 percent.
The data were strong, economists said, but not powerful enough to prompt an unpopular monetary policy tightening just before the election.
"The government has a long-standing inflation target of 2.5 percent and they are still well away from that," said Kevin Gardiner, UK economist at Morgan Stanley in London.
"But they are showing no signs of taking the policy action necessary to achieve that target. It is worrying, and has been worrying for the last couple of years."
The 2.5 percent target is for underlying inflation.

While seasonal factors such as the recent cold weather's effect on fresh produce prices accounted for some the the extra price pressures, economists said that more substantial factors, such as higher housing, oil and motoring costs, were a concern.
Motoring expenditure was up 0.9 percent in January, unchanged from December.
Jonathan Loynes, an economist at HSBC Markets said the main problem was the rise in services inflation, which was up 3.2 percent compared with up 2.9 percent in January.
He noted that "non-shop' servcies, such as insurance costs, had jumped particularly strongly.
"Overall, the numbers are undeniably disappointing, " Loynes said. "But they are partially offset by clear signs that consumers continue to demand value for money in the high street."

The inflation data came on the background of a predictably hawkish Bank of Endland inflation report on Wednesday, which called for a modest tightening of monetary policy and warned that inflation would be close to three percent and rising in two years' time.
Philip Uglow, economist at Union Plc, said the retail proce numbers would addd more credence to the Bank's view.
But with an election due by May, economists were very doubtful that Chancellor Kenneth Clarke would raise rates.
Some analysts said the breakdown of Thursday's data supported the argument for steady rates.
"But for the bad weather effects on food... underlying inflation would have fallen," said Jeremy Hawkins at Bank America in London.
"The data... should help ease any inflation worries tiggered by the jump in earnings growth reported yesterday."
The Office for National Statistics said on Wednesday that average earnings grew 4.25 percent in the year to December -- higher than market expectations.
David Coleman, chief economist at CIBC, also said the RPI report was not unduly worrying.

"Some of the largest price increases in January.. seem more like one-off factors rather than being related to the strength of consumer spending," he said, citing excise duties on tobacco, annual fare increases for travel, and bad weather for food.
"No need to panic," Coleman added.
